en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery, Volume Three, Section 51, states:
“...up until it is not yet severed. Once severed, there is ultimately no further severing; it is not something apart [from that].”
The bonds are severed.
Regarding the three aspects of the contact of liberation (*vimukti-sparśa*),
the first is a brief indication.
Second, the detailed exposition;
third, the refutation. Within the detailed exposition, there are two parts.
First, the extensive explanation of what preceded.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is associated with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
Below, [the text] reconciles contradictions; the extensive explanation of the preceding has two parts.
First, the extensive nature;
second, the extensive activity.
Since these follow the arising of the mind, they are explained below. Within the extensive nature, there are two parts.
First, it is extensively explained as the differentiation and transformation of the threefold conjunction;
later, it is extensively explained as having the nature of the mind and mental factors contacting their objects.
Regarding the first [of these two], there are further two parts.
First, the three—the conjunction, the differentiation, and the transformation—are explained individually;
subsequently, they are synthesized in the treatise.
Regarding the power of the transformation of the faculties and so forth, within the first [section] there are again three [parts].
First, an explanation of the threefold harmony;
second, an explanation of transformation;
third, an explanation of discrimination.
Because the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three is not within one's own power, it was explained separately before;
only later is "discrimination" (vikalpa) defined. In this context, "discrimination" refers to the arising of mental images that give rise to verbal expression.
For what reason is it not stated that [volition] is the cause of speech?

Because the example of the result [of speech] manifests as being remote from the conceptualization [of volition]. As for "volition causing the mind," this refers to grasping the primary causes and so forth. For what reason are faith and the other [faculties] mentioned?
Thus, [the mind] is virtuous by nature; herein, the threefold conjunction possesses the capacity to produce mental factors, which is termed "transformation.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is without transformation.
How can there be the functional capacity of mental factors (*caitta*) in that which has arisen?
This is now explained:
this is based on the threefold transformation of conditioned objects.
If it were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the mind would undergo two kinds of transformation due to its conditions;

however, the unconditioned lacks the functional capacity for transformation. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that based on the unconditioned, there are transformations of states characterized by concealment and manifestation.
This is because conditioned phenomena possess a nature subject to transformation, whereas unconditioned phenomena do not;

thus, while the latter are said to possess "functional capacity" (*śakti*) in terms of their distinct states, they lack functional capacity in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*). For example, the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its root, as well as its object and support.
In the explanation that contact is the conjunction of two,
within the commentary on action,
the general text is first explained.
The *Utpādanirodha-sūtra* states below,
citing the sūtra to establish the proof; there are two parts to reconciling contradictions regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The first assembly is the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
and the subsequent assembly is the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
These explain the "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).
And at that time, they are equal in terms of their basis,
their object, and their substance;
if considered according to their essential nature.
Alternatively, all phenomena such as names and so forth lack intrinsic nature,
because they take a single object as their common cognitive support and are therefore distinct from the actual thing itself.
If images were similar in terms of names and so forth, what would be their single nature?
Non-conceptual wisdom takes suchness as its object; being shadowless, it cannot be similar [to an image].
Since they are not identical,
we know that for that which possesses a substantial essence,
the reflection is termed "similar."
The identity of names is based on their essence.
If there were no essence, then the identity of names would consist merely in their similarity as conditioned phenomena.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as an object of cognition is one in name and one in substance;
since this is based on actual objects of cognition, there is no contradiction.
There are two types of that which obscures the mind.
First, the mind of dharmatā;
second, the dependent mind. This applies by analogy to the mental factors as well.
One should reflect on why the first master does not provide an analogy for the maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth;
the reason each case lacks an analogy is that their meanings differ.

Why is it that for the three—contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and volition (*cetanā*)—it is said they are "equal to the mind" (*cittasama*), whereas feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are not? [Because they are] ultimately unwholesome (*paramārthākuśala*).
That is to say, regarding the flow and revolution of birth and death (*saṃsāra-pravṛtti*):

for what reason is it said to serve as the basis for the untainted (*anāsrava*), while it is stated that the wholesome and the defiled (*kuśala-kliṣṭa*) are contradictory and thus cannot both serve as its basis?
This is illustrated by the case of the mental factors (*caitta*).
The third master says:
By means of the analogy of the six meanings,
one should now examine the intent of the fourth master’s objection.
It is not analogous to being accompanied by *vijñapti* (cognition) or *vedanā* (feeling);
rather, it is analogous to the six gates.
Although there may be an objection stating that contact (*sparśa*) is simultaneous with contact, [it is not so].
Since it is permitted that these five dharmas are analogous,
all three interpretations agree that while the Arhat does not abandon the *ālaya* (storehouse), he only abandons the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) as the mind-king (*cittarāja*).
It is not the name of that which is abandoned by the mind;
it is the reason why it is not the name of that which is abandoned by the mind.
The preceding example is like this.
If it were not so, why would the intermediate path be cited as an example?
This [position] takes the first two explanations as correct, along with the fourth.
Within the refutation, there are ten points.
First, a general negation;
second, a counter-interrogation;
third, the difficulty of not allowing for perfuming.
Fourth, the refutation regarding the susceptibility to being perfumed;
fifth, the rescue by another;
sixth, the further interrogation.
7. His explanation; 8.
The correct objection;
9. The turning of the question.
Section Ten: Clarifying the Thesis. Fourth, the refutation through hypothetical arguments regarding the capacity to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) consists of five parts:
first, the fault of each [moment] becoming six entities;
second, the fault of many causes producing a single effect.
1. The fault of five or three kinds of uselessness; 2.
The fault of the four powers and so forth not being in their proper order;
3. The fault of the six fruits arising simultaneously.
Furthermore, that which was stated [by him] is a counter-question;
it is by means of these [arguments].
This is the application of the principle.
Among the three metaphors for constant revolution,
the first is the metaphor of drifting between the two realms of existence.
2. The analogy of waves arising when encountering conditions;
3. The analogy of drifting objects, internal and external.
Who other than a Buddha could bring these to rest?
There are four types of Sarvāstivādins;
among them, there are four kinds [of distinctions]:
difference in essence (*jāti*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), state (*avasthā*), and relative dependence (*apekṣā*).
The third [position], based on function (*kāritra*),
establishes the existence of the time periods as most excellent,
as in the twentieth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the refutation of the doctrines of the Sthaviras and others concerning causality and related matters, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of their tenets;
second, the actual refutation. Within the presentation of their tenets, there are three sections.
First, a general heading;
second, a detailed exposition;
third, a concluding summary.
Thus, the section below on cause and effect and so forth specifically reveals three points:
first, citing extreme speed to clarify the duration;
second, citing a single entity to establish two.
Third, by citing two [scriptural] authorities, it is shown that both [theories] exist. The formal refutation consists of seven parts:
first, a general negation followed by the raising of an inquiry;
second, the manifestation of contradictions to refute the worldly [position].
1. Questioning whether the three concentrations exist or not;
2. Granting that cessation exists while cross-examining it; 3.
The sequence being contradictory while the essence is one.
Sixth, each point is examined individually, showing that their principles are contradictory.
Seventh, the conclusion summarizes and restates the intent of the objection:
Prajñāpāramitā disparages the bodhisattva by not permitting entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that four types of persons do not establish the ālayavijñāna, nor do they fall back from it or enter into it;
does this not contradict [the previous statements]?
Among these three explanations, [the former] conforms to this [latter].
The first master takes this as evidence that one does not enter the eighth stage [directly]; therefore,
he does not allow for taking the direct path to the eighth stage.
Because it is what the Buddha has condemned,
those who take a circuitous route are called "non-retrogressive.
Second, it clarifies that those who go directly are called "non-retrogressive."
There are two interpretations.
One says that "yoga" is correct;
the Buddha rebuked those who indulge in it with attachment.
Because there is no benefit [in that], it is not the case that they do not enter; furthermore, this correctly interprets the sūtra.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks based on the maturation of those who are non-regressive.
Because he had already entered it previously, he does not enter it again when it is subsequently censured.
Due to his mastery, it is said that he does not regress from the meditative absorption,
yet in reality, he does not enter it.
Regarding the names *bodhisattvabhūmi*, *alpa*, *mahat*, *vipula*, *caryā*, and so forth,
the third chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the seventy-eighth section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state:
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, regarding the afflictions that arise within the various stages for these bodhisattvas,
what are their characteristics, what are their faults, and what are their virtues? Noble son, they have the characteristic of being non-defiled."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas, within the first stage (bhūmi),
have in truth already thoroughly mastered and penetrated the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena.
For this reason, a bodhisattva gives rise to afflictions only when they are aware of them,
not out of ignorance; therefore,
it is said that this is characterized by the absence of defilement.
Because it does not produce suffering within one's own person, there is no fault; rather,
when a bodhisattva gives rise to such afflictions,
they are able to sever the causes of suffering within the realm of sentient beings.
Therefore, those immeasurable merits are most marvelous;
the unsurpassed enlightenment of the World-Honored One possesses such great merit and benefit.
Even the afflictions that arise in bodhisattvas surpass the roots of virtue of all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;
how much more so their other immeasurable merits? For what reason does the mind pervade all stages?
In that case, one should explain "according to the meaning" (*yathārtha*);

however, since maturation (*vipāka*) also extends through all stages, why does it not say "according to the meaning"? Furthermore, since "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) has already been explained separately, why must it be mentioned again?
According to the *Nirābhāsasamata-sūtra*,
the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) is the self-nature consciousness,
which is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, it is known that the stainless [consciousness] comprises two types.
Now, the fundamental consciousness has eighteen names. The verse says:
Non-perishing, fundamental, abode, storehouse, seed, stainless, support, and object-condition.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the basis for the manifestation, appearance, and transformation of the mind; it is different from [ordinary] consciousness,
the source of all births, existing from beginningless time,
and the universal support for all phenomena.

"From this arise the various realms of existence and the realization of nirvāṇa. Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that "it has existed since beginningless time," this indicates that there is no initial limit to the nature of this consciousness.
The "elements" (dhātu) are the causes;
that is, the seed-consciousness.
Of what, then, are they the causal seeds?
This refers to all phenomena;
they are called the "equal basis" because they are capable of sustaining [them].
Because it is not of the nature of a cause.
The meaning of being able to sustain is the meaning of being a support;
it does not mean the sense of being a cause.
Because the nature of the supported and the supporter are each distinct.
If it were otherwise, the term "realm" (*dhātu*) would already have conveyed that meaning.
What need is there for further words?
The meaning of these two lines is as follows: "Since beginningless time."
This reveals the general statement that the nature of this consciousness has no beginning.
It is the realm of all phenomena,
meaning it serves as the causal condition for contaminated phenomena.
It serves as the basis for the untainted dharmas and so forth;
because of the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), there are the various realms of existence (gati),
and this is due to those [untainted dharmas] serving as the basis.
There is the realization of nirvana,
which is partially similar to the second section of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
though with slight differences.
This can be understood from the text.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*—the consciousness that contains the seeds of all phenomena—there are three interpretations.
One states: here, only the name of the "container" (*ālaya*) is mentioned.
This is not because it possesses the meaning of "store" (*pitaka*);

rather, it is because it is contrasted with the *prakṛti-viśuddha* (the luminous nature) which is capable of storing [impurities]. Second, it is said that within this [treatise], all three baskets (*tri-piṭaka*) are fully present;
by citing the "storing capacity" (*saṃgraha-pitaka*), the "nature of that which is stored" (*saṃgṛhīta-svabhāva*) is revealed.

Because the seeds of affliction serve as mutual conditions for one another, it possesses the three meanings of "store" (*ālaya*) in the sense that it is maintained by these [seeds] and internally grasped as a self.
This preceding twofold interpretation is stated in the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the treatise. As for the third meaning:
While the *ālayavijñāna* is conventionally established based on its being "appropriated" (*upādāna*), it is here established based on its capacity for "storing" (*āśraya*).
This is because it possesses great sovereignty and appears to be permanent and unitary.
It is distinct from "me.

The intended meaning of its being designated as "appropriated by self-love" (*ātmasneha-parigṛhīta*) is precisely that it is called the *ālaya* because it is that which is appropriated. If one explains the *ālaya* as that which appropriates (*ālīyate*), [it refers to the fact that the seeds and the body are stored within it].
The name "Buddha-fruit" (buddhatva) should be applied [to these stages]. If explained according to the meanings of "that which conceals" (nāśraya) and "that which is concealed" (nāśrita),
then the Arhats of the two vehicles and those from the eighth stage onward should also receive this name.
Therefore, it is only that which is grasped as a storehouse (ālaya) that is named *ālayavijñāna*;
if this is lacking, it is not so.
Now, by citing its capacity to store, we manifest the storehouse of defilement (*saṃkleśa-ālaya*).
The Buddha alone possesses the single capacity for concealment (*saṃgūhana*).
Those beyond training in the Two Vehicles and those from the eighth stage onward possess two capacities [for concealment].
Beyond these, there are three types of treasuries (*pitaka*).
Therefore, it is named *ālaya* because it is that which is "appropriated" (*ā-cita*). In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
among the explanations of the "self," the treatise establishes the formal name based solely on the ultimate realization of the fruit.
The correct designation also applies to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth; thus,
it is logical that those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) are included therein,
as they are subsumed accordingly within both the stages and the pre-stages.

The *Nirnaya* (Decisive Treatise) states that those of the two vehicles who are born in the formless realm believe there is an eighth [consciousness] through which they attain entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
it clarifies that this is also taught for them,
yet it is not the definitive [teaching].
Because they ultimately cannot attain the great fruit,
this [teaching] is excluded herein.
"I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant" means:
Wu-xing’s commentary states:

"Those who harbor the view of self are not shown [this teaching], for fear that they will engage in conceptual discrimination and cling to it as a self. How could such people be allowed to engage in conceptual discrimination and clinging?"
Because its mode of activity remains uniform and unchanging until the very limit of birth and death,
it cannot be explained to those of the two vehicles or to ordinary beings of fixed nature who have not yet eliminated their innate views.

Fearing that it would increase conceptual views, he did not explain it to those who have not attained the state of an Arya. Now, the objection is raised: if [the teaching] was not given because ordinary beings possess innate views, [then why is it taught to others?]
It should also be taught to those of the two vehicles who have already severed [the afflictions].
If it is taught to those who are not deluded regarding the Dharma,
then even ordinary beings of fixed nature may likewise be non-deluded.
Why was it not taught?
Therefore, we know that it was not the correct teaching for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although [the Buddha] stated that those who harbor the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) are not to be instructed, this does not mean it was not taught at all.
This is not a statement that exhausts the full meaning of the principle.
Furthermore, regarding this treatise’s statement that [ignorance] obstructs the arising of the noble path,
it is indeed possible for an ordinary person to possess such a determinate nature.
It is the same as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This is because the bodies of non-noble ones further obstruct the noble path.
Moreover, although it was not taught even to the noble ones of the two vehicles.
For the most part, because they are not deluded regarding the Dharma,
they are not the same as ordinary beings;
this intention is not stated as a definitive teaching.
It is not that they are not explained together.
Within the Buddha’s words on the accomplishment of the Mahāyāna,
there are ten measures (*pramāṇa*) in the treatise.
Within the first four pairs,
the addition of the term "acceptance of the Mahāyāna" serves to exclude cases where either one [of the two criteria] is not established.
Because the teaching is subsumed as the primary thesis, four causes are established.
Within the seven causes that provide proof,
there are further three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the initial non-recording [of the Buddha's silence].

One interpretation states: If the Mahāyāna were taught by one dwelling within their own school as a discourse for the purpose of extensively destroying the true Dharma, the Buddha should have predicted this beforehand;
for the Buddha is always possessed of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
It is like the phenomenon of cessation.
Furthermore, it is because one constantly and correctly exerts effort to guard the True Dharma;
and furthermore, it is because one possesses knowledge of the future that is unattached and unimpeded.
Furthermore, there is another measure which states:
"There is a phenomenon as previously described;
it is said that the Buddha should have first distinguished and predicted it."
This is because it is originated by those who later destroy the True Dharma,
just like the event of the extinction of the True Dharma;
it is like the teaching that instructs a donkey to wear a lion’s skin.
There are seven types of inference.
In the twentieth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
it is stated that the Mahāyāna teachings are the word of the Buddha by means of ten reasons.
First, it did not arise previously;
this is the first reason.
Second, it cannot be known now.
Thus, this second [category] has three reasons:
it performs much that is harmful,
and it constitutes an extremely heavy obstacle.
That which is absent herein [is not included] because the five [aggregates] are not the objects of vitarka and vicāra;
thus, this is the third reason.
Sixth, because it realizes great enlightenment;
thus, if there were a Mahāyāna cause within the fifth reason.
Seventh, because it avoids the fault of a third vehicle.
8. Because if this did not exist, there would be no omniscience;
thus, within this fifth [point], there is no cause for the Mahāyāna.
9. Because there is an antidote.
This is precisely the sixth reason:
because one should not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression.
This is precisely the seventh reason.
Regarding these seven reasons,
each should further be examined through the application of inference (*anumāna*).
The Sthavira masters establish the ninefold wheel of consciousness (*citta-cakra*).

1. The life-constituent (bhavanga), 2. the ability to project [a new existence], 3. seeing, 4. thorough seeking, 5. thorough examination, 6. establishing, 7. functional activity, 8. turning back toward the object, and 9. the life-constituent.
In reality, however, there are only eight minds;
yet, speaking in terms of their cyclical succession, they are collectively said to be nine.
Thus, they constitute the wheel of the nine minds. For instance, at the very moment of initial birth, one is as yet unable to discern.
When the mind simply turns toward an object by its own natural momentum, it is called the "constituent-of-existence" mind (*bhavāṅga-citta*).
When an object arrives and the mind intends to perceive it, a state of alertness arises;

this is called the "inducing" [mind]. Once the mind has turned toward that object, it sees and illuminates it. Having seen it, it then searches for it, examining whether it is wholesome or unwholesome. Having examined it, it finally penetrates it thoroughly, cognizing its wholesomeness or unwholesomeness.

Having established the mind, one gives rise to verbal conceptualization to distinguish between its good and evil aspects. Following upon that good or evil, there arises the momentum of activity and mental engagement. Once such activity has arisen and one intends to cease it, the mind again turns back toward the previously performed actions. Having turned back toward them, it then returns to the state of "having parts" (*sabhāga*), spontaneously engaging with its objects.
These are called the nine consciousnesses;

only then does the meaning of a "wheel" (cakra) become established. Among them, the seeing-consciousness (dassana-citta) pertains to all six types of sense-consciousness, while the others pertain only to the mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa). The life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) pertains to both death and rebirth.

If one dies with a mind directed toward objects of attachment, one attains death only through that object. If one is free from desire, at the time of death there is only the "partially active" mind (*vibhaṅga-citta*);
since there is no self-love, there is nothing toward which the mind can turn, and thus no longing arises.
One who has not yet abandoned desire dies with a mind directed toward objects of attachment,
because there is a transformation of craving;
if an object were present, the mind would arise.
If there were no distinct objects, the functioning of the *savikalpaka* (discriminating) consciousness would proceed spontaneously and in continuous succession;
however, the occurrence of "seeing" (*darśana*) and "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) is not fixed in their temporal sequence.
As stated in the second volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*:
The five consciousnesses have no discernment regarding phenomena;
previously, "seeing" was said to refer to the mind.
Furthermore, it is stated that seeing merely illuminates, which serves to exclude the preceding mind.
Regarding the statement that the five desires are not a locus for attachment:
even when one is born in the two higher realms, the consciousness of "I" still arises.
In the first proof, it refers to the mind that arises through accumulation.
Furthermore, it is explained that because it is the cause for the arising and production of phenomena from the seeds accumulated within its locus,
it is called "mind" (*citta*).
Within the "Analysis of Matter" (*Rūpa-bhaṅga*) and the section on "Mental Factors Dissociated from Mind" (*Citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*),
there should also be a mind that arises from seeds that are neither defiled nor pure; however,
this has been omitted for brevity.
If you claim that such categories are merely provisional and cannot sustain the real seeds of internal dharmas—
just as in the first fascicle it was stated that provisional things like embankments block real water—
why should this case be any different? One might argue that it is plausible for provisional things to temporarily obstruct and suppress [the seeds].

It is not yet possible to definitively maintain that this principle [applies] in all cases. If that were so, then the *prātimokṣa* vows and other such precepts would also be definitively prohibited for the Buddha’s body;
in what sense, then, are they not the same? "Prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) has the meaning of "ceasing."
The provisional can conceal the real;
"holding" has the meaning of "taking up.
Therefore, the provisional does not hold.
Refuting Bhāviveka’s pseudo-inference:
the thesis contains the fallacy of the non-establishment of the qualified object (*viśeṣya-asiddha*),
as in the case of the *paramārtha* of the Middle Way discussed in the treatise.
Furthermore, there is the fault of contradicting one's own tenets;
it does not establish [the point] as explained in the commentary. Regarding the "common example" (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) of being like an illusion:
Regarding the two proofs based on conventional truth that [things] are like illusions:
since the actual reality of being "like an illusion" is not produced through conditions, the logical reason (hetu) cannot be established.
Like an illusion, it appears as a thing;
this thesis is not unestablished, for it is posited by means of emptiness in accordance with ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
According to both of these schools, all phenomena are ineffable;
they are neither empty nor non-empty,
and neither dependently originated nor not dependently originated.
How can things such as flowers in the sky be used as metaphors?
Since the corroborative example (sapakṣa) would likewise suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished for both parties,
it is termed a pseudo-inference (ābhāsa-anumāna).
In the second proof, it is established that the body and the environment do not exist apart from the mind.
This corresponds to the fifth proof among the eight proofs regarding karmic results;
therein, within the discussion of rebirth destinies, the "five destinies" are mentioned.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that because the asuras are excessively deceitful and fraudulent, they are called "non-gods" (*asura*).
In certain sūtras, they are categorized as one of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
In reality, they belong to the heavenly realm;
thus, there are five destinies (*gati*).
Other sūtras also state that they are included within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
This is because it conforms to the principle;
alternatively, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* speaks from the perspective of the majority,
whereas in reality it pertains to both destinies.
As in the first fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
regarding the phrase "arising without confusion":
this may be so in terms of the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*).
Just as there are five destinies and four modes of birth in the desire realm, what are they?
They are the afflictions, karma, and fruits that are definitively associated with these destinies and modes of birth.
Furthermore, it is said that there is a mixture [of results];
for example, as a heavy [karma] may be made light,
there are those who experience the fruits of the evil destinies within the six heavens of the desire realm.
Humans and devas also give rise to afflictions such as discrimination;
furthermore, there are those who receive distinct retributions for their wholesome karma in the evil realms,
such as dragons, elephants, horses, and other meritorious spirits among humans and devas.
None of these have a fixed affiliation.
Now, it might be argued that what arises as something else could be called "confused"; however, this interpretation is not correct, for they lack a fixed affiliation.
Only the eighth consciousness has a fixed destiny of rebirth that cannot be altered;
since the alteration of such a destiny pertains only to specific retributions and the like,
the others are termed "mixed."
Because one does not know which realm or class of beings [the deceased] will go to, if such a thought arises, it is termed "mixed.
The eighth [thought] is not so; therefore, it is called "unmixed."
Regarding the arising of innate wholesome states and the results of karma associated with the mental consciousness without intermixture:
just as with innate wholesome states,
although these belong specifically to the desire realm, they likewise possess a fixed determination.
The destinies and births are called "unmixed" [only] in this sense; otherwise, it would not be so.
It is only the fruit of mental karma that is unmixed.
This is a designation based on its characteristics.
"It is not that it is unreal and without admixture;
